subject: english-language
title: Methods in Action Adventure
welcome_lead: Now apply the methods — analysing HOW writers create specific effects.
meta_desc: GCSE English Language methods applied — analysing word choice, sentence structure for effect.
final_note: You practised analysing how word, sentence and structural choices combine to shape reader response.

concepts.def: What the chosen method makes us feel/think
How a paragraph builds and ends
A move from one idea to another
Placing opposing ideas to highlight difference
What the writer directs our attention

walkthroughs.body_html: Don't just SPOT the method — show what it DOES. 'The verb shattered creates a violent, irreversible sense of loss.'

Notice WHERE in the paragraph the method appears.

Opening = sets the scene. Middle = develops. End = lingers in the reader's mind.

Pairing 'roaring laughter' with 'sudden silence' makes the silence feel HEAVIER by contrast.

Always ask: what's it set against?

A group of words from a similar area of meaning — e.g. 'whisper, scream, mumble, shout' all belong to the semantic field of vocalisation.
A semantic field is a field of study like physics or biology.

Bruner was a nativist who opposed all social theories.
A morpheme is a syllable.
The smallest unit of meaning in a language — a word like 'unhappiness' has three morphemes: un-, happy, and -ness.

mcqs.q: How does Bruner's view of language acquisition differ from Vygotsky's?
options: Bruner was a nativist who opposed all social theories.
A morpheme is a sound that has no meaning.

Both emphasise social interaction, but Bruner proposes a Language Acquisition Support System (LASS) — adults provide structured, predictable interaction (book-reading, peekaboo) that 'scaffolds' acquisition. Vygotsky's scaffolding is broader (within ZPD across all learning).
Bruner and Vygotsky are saying the same thing with different names.
